Not applicable - intravenous use under fasting/anesthetic conditions

summary: Thiopental sodium is an ultra-short-acting barbiturate given intravenously to induce general anesthesia and as a supplement for short procedures, and to control status epilepticus and raised intracranial pressure. Its rapid onset and brief action reflect quick brain uptake and redistribution. It depresses respiration and the cardiovascular system, can cause laryngospasm, and is contraindicated in porphyria. It is a controlled substance (Schedule III) and is habit-forming.
indications: Sole anesthetic for brief procedures of short duration
Supplementation of regional anesthesia or other anesthetic agents
Control of convulsive states / refractory status epilepticus
Reduction of raised intracranial pressure in neurosurgical or head-injury patients (controlled ventilation)

dosage.d: 3-5 mg/kg IV (test dose 25-75 mg, then titrate); usual 100-150 mg over 10-15 s
dosage.n: Reduce in elderly, debilitated, hypovolemic, or premedicated patients

dosage.d: 75-125 mg (3-5 mL of 2.5%) IV as soon as possible after seizure begins
dosage.n: Repeat / infusion with airway control and monitoring
Requires controlled ventilation and intensive monitoring

dosage.c: Renal or hepatic impairment / elderly / debilitated

admin: For intravenous use only, by personnel trained in anesthesia with resuscitation equipment immediately available
Reconstitute and use as a freshly prepared solution (commonly 2.5%); discard unused solution
Inject slowly and titrate to clinical effect; avoid extravasation and intra-arterial injection (can cause severe arterial spasm and gangrene)
Maintain a patent airway and be prepared to support ventilation
Do not mix in the same line with acidic drugs (e.g., succinylcholine, atropine) - incompatibility
moa: Thiopental is a thiobarbiturate that enhances and prolongs the action of the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA at the GABA-A receptor, increasing chloride conductance and depressing the central nervous system. Its lipophilicity gives very rapid CNS penetration and onset; the short clinical effect results from redistribution from brain to other tissues. It also reduces cerebral metabolic rate and intracranial pressure.

absolute: Variegate porphyria or acute intermittent porphyria
Absence of suitable veins / inability to give intravenously
relative: Severe cardiovascular disease, shock, or hypovolemia
Severe respiratory disease or airway obstruction
Increased blood urea, myxedema, severe anemia
monitor: Blood pressure and heart rate / ECG

preg: Thiopental crosses the placenta and can cause neonatal respiratory depression; use in pregnancy (including obstetric anesthesia) only when clearly needed, at the lowest effective dose, with neonatal resuscitation available.
lact: Thiopental is excreted in breast milk in small amounts. After a single anesthetic dose, breastfeeding can usually resume once the mother is awake and alert; some clinicians advise briefly withholding nursing.
renal: Effects may be increased and prolonged in renal impairment; reduce the dose and titrate slowly.
hepatic: Thiopental is metabolized by the liver; effects may be exaggerated and prolonged in hepatic impairment. Reduce the dose and use with caution.

major: Other CNS depressants - opioids, benzodiazepines, alcohol, inhaled anesthetics (additive sedation and respiratory depression)
moderate: Chronic enzyme inducers (may reduce effect over time)
minor: Oral contraceptive efficacy (barbiturate enzyme induction with chronic use)
interactions.food: Not applicable for intravenous anesthetic use
interactions.alcohol: Acute alcohol increases CNS and respiratory depression; chronic use can induce tolerance - avoid
interactions.diagnostics: May affect EEG (burst suppression at high dose) used to guide therapy

serious: Severe tissue injury from extravasation or intra-arterial injection (necrosis, gangrene)

monitoring: Continuous monitoring of airway, respiration, and oxygenation
Blood pressure, heart rate, and ECG
EEG when used for status epilepticus or ICP control
counsel: This medicine is given by injection by an anesthesia provider in a monitored setting
You will fall asleep within seconds; tell the team about all medicines and any allergy to barbiturates
You may feel drowsy and clumsy for the rest of the day - do not drive or operate machinery for 24 hours
Avoid alcohol and other sedatives during recovery
Report any pain at the injection site during administration
pk: Loss of consciousness within ~10-40 seconds of IV injection (one arm-brain circulation)
Distribution very short; elimination half-life ~3-12 hours (longer with repeated/high dosing)
Single induction dose lasts ~5-10 minutes (terminated by redistribution)
Store dry powder below 25 C; use reconstituted solution promptly and discard unused portion
pearls: Habit forming: Yes - controlled substance (Schedule III); risk of dependence and abuse
Short clinical action is due to redistribution, not metabolism; repeated dosing leads to accumulation and prolonged recovery
Contraindicated in porphyria - can precipitate an acute attack
Intra-arterial injection can cause severe arterial spasm, thrombosis, and gangrene - confirm IV placement
Reduces cerebral metabolic rate and intracranial pressure, useful in neuroanesthesia
missed: Not applicable - thiopental is administered as single intravenous doses by an anesthesia provider during a procedure, not as a self-administered scheduled medication.
overdose: Overdose causes profound respiratory and cardiovascular depression, apnea, hypotension, hypothermia, and coma. There is no specific antidote. Management is supportive with airway protection and mechanical ventilation, oxygen, intravenous fluids and vasopressors for hypotension, and intensive monitoring; hemodialysis or hemoperfusion may be considered in severe cases.
